title: Designing a REST API
goal: Design a clean REST API on paper before writing code: resources, URLs, verbs, status codes and error shapes.

concepts: Resources are nouns (/tasks), verbs come from HTTP methods
Collection vs item URLs: /tasks and /tasks/:id; nesting /projects/:id/tasks
A consistent error format: { error: { code, message, details } }
Filtering, sorting and pagination with query params
Idempotency: GET, PUT and DELETE can be repeated safely; POST can't

build.task: In api-starter, write docs/api-design.md for a 'Task Manager API' with projects and tasks: every endpoint (method, URL, purpose), example request and response bodies, status codes for success and each failure, query parameters for filtering tasks (status, priority, due before), sorting (sort=dueDate or sort=-priority) and pagination (page, limit), and the response envelope for lists ({ data, meta: { page, limit, total } }). Define one error format used everywhere. List which endpoints are idempotent and why.

starterFiles.name: docs/api-design.md
starterFiles.content:
# Task Manager API design

## Resources
- Project: { id, name, createdAt }
- Task: { id, projectId, title, status, priority, dueDate, createdAt, updatedAt }

## Endpoints
| Method | URL | Purpose | Success | Errors |
|---|---|---|---|---|

## List responses

## Error format

## Query parameters

## Idempotency

acceptance: All CRUD endpoints for projects and tasks, including nested /projects/:id/tasks
Every endpoint lists success and error status codes
Example JSON for at least one request and response per resource
One consistent error format, used in every example
Filtering, sorting and pagination documented with examples
Idempotency section explains GET/PUT/DELETE vs POST

hints: Use plural nouns, no verbs in URLs: POST /tasks, not /createTask. Actions that don't fit CRUD can be sub-resources, e.g. POST /tasks/:id/complete, used sparingly.
400 = malformed input; 404 = doesn't exist; 409 = conflicts with current state (e.g. duplicate name); 422 is sometimes used for validation errors. Pick one convention and stick to it.
201 responses should include the created resource and ideally a Location: /tasks/123 header.

explainBack.q: Why is POST /tasks better than POST /createTask?
lookFor: HTTP method already says the action

explainBack.q: What does idempotent mean? Give an example from your design.
lookFor: repeating the request has the same effect as once

explainBack.q: Why use one error format for every endpoint?
lookFor: clients handle errors in one place

lastHintExplanation: In REST, URLs name resources and HTTP methods say what to do with them, so the API is predictable. An idempotent request has the same effect whether sent once or many times: DELETE /tasks/5 twice still leaves task 5 deleted, but POST /tasks twice creates two tasks. One error format lets frontends handle every failure the same way.

predict.q: A client sends PUT /tasks/7 with the same body three times. How many changes happen?
options: Same final state as one request (idempotent)
predict.why: PUT replaces the resource with the same data each time.

title: Structuring an Express app: routers, controllers, services
goal: Organise an Express API into layers so it stays clean as it grows.

concepts: express.Router() to group routes by resource
Layers: routes (HTTP wiring) → controllers (req/res) → services (business logic) → data
Why services shouldn't know about req/res
Mounting routers: app.use('/api/tasks', tasksRouter)
Route-level middleware (e.g. only on some routes)
Folder structure by feature: src/tasks/{tasks.routes,tasks.controller,tasks.service}.ts

build.task: In api-starter, implement the projects part of your Day 91 design with in-memory storage, structured by feature: src/projects/projects.routes.ts, projects.controller.ts, projects.service.ts and projects.repo.ts (in-memory Map behind an interface, so PostgreSQL can replace it later). Mount it at /api/projects. Add a requestId middleware that sets an X-Request-Id header and includes it in logs. Services throw typed errors (NotFoundError, ConflictError for duplicate names) that the error middleware maps to your Day 91 error format and status codes.
acceptance: Feature folder with routes, controller, service and repo files
Service and repo have no req/res or Express imports
Repo implements an interface (ProjectsRepo) so it can be swapped later
Duplicate project name returns 409; missing returns 404, in your error format
Every response has X-Request-Id, and logs include it

hints: interface ProjectsRepo { list(): Promise<Project[]>; get(id: string): Promise<Project | undefined>; create(p: NewProject): Promise<Project>; ... } Make methods async now, so switching to a database later doesn't change callers.

Error classes: class AppError extends Error { constructor(public status: number, public code: string, message: string) { super(message) } } then class NotFoundError extends AppError { constructor(what: string) { super(404, 'NOT_FOUND', `${what} not found`) } }.
Request id: import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto'; res.locals.requestId = randomUUID(); res.setHeader('X-Request-Id', res.locals.requestId); next();
proof: Commit with the projects feature folder.

explainBack.q: Walk through POST /api/projects through each layer.
lookFor: service applies rules (duplicate check) and calls repo

explainBack.q: Why should services not import Express?
lookFor: HTTP is just one way in

lastHintExplanation: Each layer has one job: the router maps URLs to controllers; the controller translates HTTP into function calls and results into responses; the service holds business rules; the repo talks to storage. Because services don't know about Express, you can test them directly and call them from anywhere. Because the repo is an interface, PostgreSQL can replace the Map without touching the service.

predict.q: router.get('/:id', ...) is mounted with app.use('/api/projects', router). Which URL reaches it?
predict.why: Router paths are relative to their mount path.

title: Validation and async error handling
goal: Validate every input with zod middleware and make sure async errors always reach your error handler.

concepts: Never trust client input: validate body, params and query
A reusable validate({ body, params, query }) middleware with zod
Coercing query strings (page=2 → number) with z.coerce
Express 5 forwards rejected promises from async handlers to the error handler
Returning field-level validation errors in your error format
Unhandled rejections: why un-awaited promises crash Node

build.task: In api-starter, write src/middleware/validate.ts: validate({ body?, params?, query? }) using zod schemas, returning 400 with { error: { code: 'VALIDATION_FAILED', message, details: [{ path, message }] } }. Apply it to every projects route (params id must be a UUID; name 1–60 chars, trimmed). Make all controllers async and confirm thrown errors reach the error handler. Add a /api/debug/crash route (only when NODE_ENV=development) that throws inside an async function, to prove the error handler catches it. Add process-level handlers that log unhandledRejection and uncaughtException.
acceptance: validate() middleware is reusable and typed
Invalid body, params or query returns 400 with field-level details
Query values are coerced (e.g. ?limit=10 becomes a number)
Async errors always reach the error handler (crash route returns 500 JSON, server keeps running)
Debug route only exists in development
Process-level handlers log unexpected errors

hints: validate: const r = schema.body?.safeParse(req.body); if (r && !r.success) return next(new ValidationError(r.error.issues)); if (r) req.body = r.data; ... next();
In Express 5, req.query is a getter you can't reassign. Store parsed query values in res.locals.query instead.
z.string().trim().min(1).max(60) trims first, then checks length. z.string().uuid() validates ids.
proof: Commit with validation middleware and updated routes.

explainBack.q: Why validate on the server if the Angular form already validates?
lookFor: clients can be bypassed (curl, modified JS)

explainBack.q: What happens in Express 5 when an async handler throws, and what happened in Express 4?
lookFor: Express 5 catches rejected promises and calls the error handler
Express 4 needed try/catch or a wrapper

lastHintExplanation: Anyone can send requests straight to your API with curl, skipping the Angular form, so the server must validate everything. In Express 5, a promise rejected by an async handler is passed to your error middleware automatically. In Express 4 it wasn't, and the request would hang or crash the process unless you wrapped handlers.

predict.why: Coercion gives NaN, which fails number validation.

title: Tasks API: filtering, sorting and pagination
goal: Implement the tasks resource fully, including list queries that real frontends need.

concepts: Translating query params into filters safely (whitelists)
Sorting with a direction prefix (sort=-dueDate)
Offset pagination: page/limit → skip/take; total counts
Default and maximum limits to protect the server
PATCH for partial updates; marking tasks done
Nested routes: /api/projects/:projectId/tasks

resources.title: Microsoft: API design — filter and paginate data

build.task: In api-starter, add the tasks feature (routes/controller/service/repo, in memory) following your design: create under a project (404 if the project doesn't exist), get, PATCH (title, status, priority, dueDate), delete, and list with filters status, priority and dueBefore, sort (whitelisted fields, - for descending), page and limit (default 20, max 100). List responses use { data, meta: { page, limit, total, totalPages } }. Seed 50 sample tasks on startup in development. Write 10 curl examples in docs/tasks-examples.md.
acceptance: All task endpoints work, validated with your middleware
Filters combine (status + priority + dueBefore)
Unknown sort fields return 400; limit is capped at 100
meta values are correct (check the last page)
Creating a task for a missing project returns 404
docs/tasks-examples.md has 10 working curl examples

hints: Sort whitelist: const SORTABLE = ['dueDate', 'priority', 'createdAt', 'title'] as const; parse '-dueDate' into { field: 'dueDate', dir: 'desc' }.
Pagination: const start = (page - 1) * limit; data = filtered.slice(start, start + limit); totalPages = Math.ceil(total / limit).
query schema: z.object({ status: z.enum([...]).optional(), page: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).default(1), limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).default(20), ... }).
proof: Commit with the tasks feature and docs.

explainBack.q: Why whitelist sortable fields instead of sorting by whatever the client sends?

lastHintExplanation: When this list becomes a SQL query, a field name from the client can't be a bound parameter like a value can, so an unchecked sort field risks SQL injection. Whitelisting known fields avoids that and keeps the API predictable. Capping limit stops one request from asking for a million rows and exhausting server memory.

predict.q: total = 45, limit = 20, page = 3. How many items are in data?
predict.why: Pages 1 and 2 hold 40 items, so page 3 has the remaining 5.

title: CORS and connecting Angular to Express
goal: Connect your Angular app to your own API, understanding CORS instead of fighting it.

concepts: Same-origin policy: scheme + host + port
CORS: the server says which origins may read responses
Preflight OPTIONS requests for non-simple requests (JSON bodies, custom headers)
The cors middleware with an allowlist from env
Alternative: the Angular dev-server proxy (proxy.conf.json)
API clients: Thunder Client, Postman or Bruno collections

resources.title: Angular: Proxying to a backend server

build.task: Create a simple Angular frontend (new repo task-manager-web or inside angular-playground) that uses your api-starter: projects list and create, project page listing tasks with filters, sort and pagination (driven by query params), and create/edit/delete tasks. First call the API directly from localhost:4200 and fix CORS on the server with an allowlist read from a CORS_ORIGINS env variable. Then also set up proxy.conf.json and explain in docs/cors.md which approach you'd use in dev and in production and why. Export a Thunder Client, Postman or Bruno collection of all endpoints into the API repo.
acceptance: Angular app performs all project and task operations against your API
CORS allowlist comes from env; an unlisted origin is blocked (test it)
Preflight requests visible in the Network tab and explained in docs/cors.md
Proxy config works as an alternative
API collection file committed

hints: Server: app.use(cors({ origin: config.CORS_ORIGINS.split(','), credentials: true })). The origin must match exactly: http://localhost:4200 (no trailing slash).
In DevTools, look for an OPTIONS request before your POST or PATCH. That's the preflight; it must succeed for the real request to go through.
Proxy: proxy.conf.json { "/api": { "target": "http://localhost:4000", "secure": false } } and in angular.json serve options "proxyConfig": "proxy.conf.json". Then call /api/... from Angular.
proof: Links to both repos (or folders) and docs/cors.md.

explainBack.q: Explain what CORS protects against, and who enforces it.
lookFor: stops other websites reading responses using the user's browser

explainBack.q: Why does the proxy make CORS disappear in development?
lookFor: dev server forwards to the API
no cross-origin request from the browser's view

lastHintExplanation: The browser enforces the same-origin policy: a page from localhost:4200 can't read responses from localhost:4000 unless that server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin naming it. That protects users from other sites reading data with their cookies. curl ignores CORS. With a dev proxy, the browser only talks to 4200, and the dev server forwards requests to the API, so nothing is cross-origin.

predict.q: Server allows origin 'http://localhost:4200'. The Angular app runs on http://127.0.0.1:4200. Is it allowed?
predict.why: Origins are compared as strings; localhost and 127.0.0.1 differ.

title: Debug lab: the broken tasks API, and week review
goal: Fix CORS, middleware, async and query-string bugs in an Express API.

concepts: CORS origin strings must match exactly
Middleware that responds must not also call next()
Un-awaited promises: responses sent too early and crashes from unhandled rejections
Query string values are strings ('true' !== true)
Reproducing bugs with curl before fixing them

build.task: Copy the starter into day96-debug/ in node-playground and npm install. Expected: an Angular app on http://localhost:4200 can call the API; POST /tasks with {} returns 400 and nothing else happens; POST /tasks with title 'boom' returns 500 JSON and the server keeps running; GET /tasks?done=false returns the open tasks. There are 4 bugs. Reproduce each with curl (or a browser fetch from a page on port 4200) before fixing it, and fix each in its own commit. Write week16-notes.md (Days 91–95).

starterFiles.name: day96-debug/server.js

acceptance: Requests from http://localhost:4200 are allowed by CORS
POST {} returns 400 only; no task is created and no 'headers sent' error appears
POST 'boom' returns 500 JSON and the process keeps running
GET /tasks?done=false returns the open tasks
4 fix commits; week16-notes.md written

hints: The browser console says the CORS header value doesn't match the page's origin. Compare the two strings character by character.
After a 400, the server log shows a second error and a task with no title gets created. What happens after the response in validate()?

'boom' kills the whole server with an unhandledRejection. The handler doesn't wait for fakeDbSave. Make the handler async and await it (Express 5 will route the error to the error handler). And query values are strings: compare with done === 'true'.
proof: Link to your last fix commit.

lookFor: fakeDbSave not awaited → early 201 and crash

explainBack.q: Why did one un-awaited promise crash the whole server?
lookFor: Node exits on unhandled rejections by default

lastHintExplanation: 1) The CORS origin 'http://localhost:4200/' has a trailing slash, but browsers send 'http://localhost:4200'. 2) validate() sends a 400 and then still calls next(), so the handler runs too; return after responding. 3) fakeDbSave isn't awaited, so 201 is sent before saving, and its rejection is unhandled, which crashes Node; make the handler async and await it. 4) req.query.done is the string 'false', never the boolean false.
